title: Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP): Core
summary: Defines the core of the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP), a way of streaming XML elements between two network endpoints in close to real time. It is a general framework, but is mainly used to build instant messaging and presence systems. It was replaced by RFC 6120.

eli5.summary: Two people pass notes back and forth through an open pipe, each note in a standard envelope, so messages arrive almost instantly. That is the basic idea of XMPP chat.

subtitle: The core of XMPP: a stream of XML elements between a client and a server, with addressing, TLS, SASL and three kinds of stanza.

tldr.problem: Near-real-time messaging and presence needs an open way to send small pieces of structured data between any two network endpoints, securely and with a clear addressing scheme.
tldr.mechanism: Each side opens an XML stream over TCP, optionally secures it with TLS, authenticates with SASL, binds a resource, and then sends message, presence and iq stanzas that servers route by address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3920 was replaced by RFC 6120 and updated by RFC 6122, so it is now a historical version of the XMPP core.

today: RFC 3920 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 6120 and updated by RFC 6122, so the XMPP core is now defined there.

sections.title: What XMPP Is and How It Is Laid Out
sections.content:
The Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP) is an open XML protocol for near-real-time messaging, presence and request-response services. Its syntax and semantics were developed originally in the Jabber open-source community, mainly in 1999. In 2002 the XMPP working group was chartered to adapt it as an IETF instant messaging and presence technology. This memo defines the core features of XMPP 1.0; the instant messaging and presence extensions that meet RFC 2779 are in a companion document, RFC 3921.

XMPP is not tied to one network design, but it has usually been used in a client-server pattern. Clients connect to a server over a TCP connection, and servers connect to each other over TCP too, so the system becomes a network of inter-communicating servers. A server manages streams and routes stanzas, and most also store client data such as contact lists. A gateway is a server-side service that translates between XMPP and a foreign messaging system. Servers talking to each other is optional.

The recommended port for client-to-server connections is 5222 and for server-to-server connections 5269.
sections.eli5: Your chat app talks to a post office (the server). Post offices talk to each other, so you can send a note to a friend who uses a different one.

sections.title: Addresses: The JID
sections.content:
Every entity that can talk XMPP has an address called a Jabber Identifier (JID), written [ node "@" ] domain [ "/" resource ]. Only the domain is required.

  • The domain identifies the server or service. It SHOULD be a fully qualified domain name and MUST be an internationalized domain name.
  • The node usually names the user or other entity, such as a chat room. The bare form is node@domain.
  • The resource names one session, such as a device or location, for example node@domain/home versus node@domain/work. It is opaque to servers and other clients. An entity MAY keep several connected resources at once.

Each of the three parts MUST NOT be more than 1023 bytes, for a maximum total of 3071 bytes with the separators. Before comparing identifiers, a server MUST (and a client SHOULD) apply the matching stringprep profile: Nameprep for the domain, Nodeprep for the node and Resourceprep for the resource.
sections.eli5: A JID is like a home address with a room number: the building is the server, the person is the name, and the room is the device you are using right now.

sections.title: XML Streams and Stanzas
sections.content:
Two ideas carry everything. An XML stream is a container for exchanging XML elements between two entities: it starts with an opening <stream> tag and ends with a closing </stream> tag, and in between the sender can send an unbounded number of elements. A stanza is a discrete unit of structured information sent as a direct child of the stream. The only stanzas defined are <message/>, <presence/> and <iq/>. Elements used to negotiate TLS, SASL or dialback are not stanzas.

A stream carries data in one direction, so a client-to-server session uses two streams: the initial stream and a response stream the server MUST negotiate back. This memo binds XMPP to TCP only. For client-to-server traffic one TCP connection is shared in both directions; between servers two connections are used, one for each direction.

The stream header carries the attributes to, from, id, xml:lang and version. The id is created by the receiving entity, may be security-critical, and MUST be unpredictable and nonrepeating. A version of at least 1.0 signals support for stream features, which the receiving server then announces in a <features/> element.

Stream errors are unrecoverable. The detecting side sends an <error/> element with a defined condition such as <xml-not-well-formed/> or <host-unknown/>, closes the stream and ends the TCP connection.
sections.eli5: A stream is a long open pipe. Each little note you drop in it is a stanza. If something goes badly wrong, the pipe is shut and you start again.

sections.title: Securing the Stream: TLS, SASL and Resource Binding
sections.content:
Streams are secured in a fixed order. TLS SHOULD be used to protect the channel against tampering and eavesdropping, using a STARTTLS extension modelled on similar ones for IMAP, POP3 and ACAP. If TLS is used, it MUST finish before SASL starts, so that SASL credentials are protected. After a successful TLS negotiation the original stream is considered closed and a new stream header is sent.

SASL MUST then be used to authenticate the stream. The server advertises mechanisms in a <mechanisms/> element. The client picks one with <auth/>, and the two sides exchange <challenge/> and <response/> elements until the server sends <success/> or <failure/>, or the client sends <abort/>. Character data in these elements is base64-encoded. After <success/> a new stream is started again. An entity SHOULD NOT send stanzas before the stream is authenticated, and the receiver MUST NOT accept them.

Finally, a client binds a resource. The server offers an empty <bind/> feature, and the client sends an iq stanza of type set to bind either a resource of its choosing or one the server generates. The result is a full JID of the form node@domain/resource.
sections.eli5: First you lock the pipe so nobody can listen in. Then you show your ID at the door. Then you pick a name tag for the device you are using today.

sections.title: The Three Stanzas and How Servers Route Them
sections.content:
All three stanza kinds share five attributes: to, from, id, type and xml:lang. A server MUST either check a client's from against its connected resources or set it itself, which prevents a client from forging a sender.

  • <message/> is a push mechanism, like email: one entity pushes information to another.
  • <presence/> is a broadcast or publish-subscribe mechanism. Usually it carries no to, and the server broadcasts it to subscribers.
  • <iq/> (Info/Query) is a request-response mechanism, similar to HTTP. Its id and type are REQUIRED, and a get or set MUST be answered with a result or error that keeps the same id.

Stanza errors, unlike stream errors, are recoverable. Servers MUST process stanzas in order between any two entities. To route, a server looks at the to address. With none, it handles the stanza for the sender. A foreign domain is routed over a server-to-server stream, opening one if needed. A subdomain goes to its service. For node@domain/resource the server delivers to the exactly matching resource or returns <service-unavailable/>, and for a bare node@domain to at least one connected resource.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of notes: a plain message to someone, an announcement to everyone who follows you, and a question that needs an answer back.

sections.title: Security, Dialback and Compliance
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support "high security", meaning mutual authentication plus integrity checking, and service provisioning SHOULD use it. The required layering is TCP, then TLS, then SASL, then XMPP. At a minimum, all implementations MUST support SASL DIGEST-MD5 for authentication, TLS with the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher for confidentiality, and TLS plus SASL EXTERNAL for both. The RFC notes that SASL has no channel binding to TLS.

Between servers, a compliant server MUST support TLS and SASL, and SHOULD also support server dialback for historical reasons. Dialback has a receiving server ask the authoritative server for a domain whether a key is valid. It is not a security mechanism, gives only weak verification of server identities, is susceptible to DNS poisoning unless DNSSEC is used, and SHOULD NOT be used when SASL is. Server hostnames are resolved first with an SRV lookup for _xmpp-server._tcp, falling back to an address record on port 5269.

Clients and servers are compliant when they support XML streams with TLS, SASL and resource binding, the basic semantics of the three stanza kinds, and the related error handling. Dialback is optional for servers.
sections.eli5: Locking the pipe and showing ID are the real protection. Dialback is just a quick phone call to check the sender's story, which a clever trickster might still fool.
